s0201.literal: "Thereupon he personally donned armor, attacked fiercely on four sides; the city shook with terror; at one drum-stroke it fell; Wang Lin, Wang Guixian, Prince Fufeng Kezhuoluo Xiaoyu, Minister Lu Qian, and Left Director Li Taotu were captured alive and sent to the capital.
s0201.idiomatic: He then donned armor himself, stormed the city on four sides, and took it at the first drum-roll; Wang Lin, Wang Guixian, Prince Fufeng Kezhuoluo Xiaoyu, Minister Lu Qian, and Left Director Li Taotu were captured alive and sent to the capital.

s0202.literal: [13] Jinghe fled in fear and panic, recovering all his fine horses and baggage.
s0202.idiomatic: [13] Pi Jinghe fled in panic, gathering up his fine horses and baggage.

s0203.literal: When Lin was captured, many of his old followings were still in the army; Lin had always won the soldiers' hearts, and those who saw him all sighed and could not look up; Mingche feared trouble and sent attendants to pursue and kill Lin, sending only his head.
s0203.idiomatic: With Lin captured, many of his old troops were still in camp; he had always won the soldiers' hearts, and onlookers wept and could not raise their eyes. Mingche feared a mutiny, sent men to pursue and kill him, and forwarded only his head.

s0204.literal: An edict said: "Shouyang is an ancient capital, girding the Huai and Ru, controlling the Yellow and Luo; he who holds it is secure—it is called a strategic hinge.
s0204.idiomatic: An edict said: "Shouyang is an ancient metropolis, commanding the Huai and Ru and the Yellow and Luo; whoever holds it is secure—it is a strategic hinge.

s0205.literal: Attendant-in-ordinary, bearer of the staff, director-general over punitive military affairs, campaign-north grand general, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, Duke of Nanping Commandery state Gong Mingche—heroic design achieved, grand strategy covering the age.
s0205.idiomatic: Attendant-in-ordinary, bearer of the staff, director-general of punitive armies, campaign-north grand general, and Duke of Nanping state Wu Mingche has shown heroic achievement and a grand strategy for the age.

s0206.literal: In former days at Tunyi he helped forge the imperial enterprise, then covered Heng and Yue, cleared miasmal vapors, truly swallowed Yunmeng, and stood on the cliffed upper stream.
s0206.idiomatic: In former days at Tunyi he helped build the imperial enterprise, covered Heng and Yue, cleared the miasmal vapors, took Yunmeng, and stood on the cliffed upper stream.

s0207.literal: Now in this pacification he has restored our royal strategy—wind moves, lightning sweeps, bold warriors race; [14] moon formations and cloud ladders, golden ramparts seized by storm; might overawes foreign lands, kindness spreads to border folk.
s0207.idiomatic: Now in this pacification he has restored our royal strategy—swift as wind and lightning, bold warriors racing; [14] with moon formations and cloud ladders he stormed golden ramparts; his might awed foreign lands and his kindness reached the border folk.

s0208.literal: Merit and ability alone fit the supreme command; lofty banners and broad rewards are the constant worthy rite—he may be director-general over military affairs in Yu, He, Jian, Guang, Shuo, North Xu, six provinces, chariots-and-cavalry grand general, and Inspector of Yu Province, with fief increased by three thousand five hundred households before enfeoffment; the rest as before.
s0208.idiomatic: Merit and ability alone fit the supreme command; lofty banners and broad rewards are the constant rite—he is appointed director-general over Yu, He, Jian, Guang, Shuo, and North Xu, chariots-and-cavalry grand general, and inspector of Yu Province, with three thousand five hundred households added to his pre-enfeoffment fief; the rest unchanged.

s0209.literal: " An edict sent Palace Usher Xiao Chunfeng [15] to Shouyang to invest Mingche; south of the city an altar was set, two hundred thousand soldiers with flags, drums, weapons, and armor arrayed; Mingche mounted the altar to receive investiture, completed the rites and withdrew; generals and soldiers all leaped for joy.
s0209.idiomatic: An edict sent palace usher Xiao Chunfeng [15] to invest Mingche at Shouyang; an altar was raised south of the city before two hundred thousand troops with flags, drums, arms, and armor; Mingche mounted the altar, received investiture, completed the rites, and withdrew amid general exultation.

s0210.literal: Initially Qin commandery belonged to Southern Yan Province; later it was attached to Qiaozhou; now an edict returned Qiao's Qin, Xuyi, and Shennong three commanderies to Southern Yan Province on Mingche's account.
s0210.idiomatic: Qin commandery had first belonged to Southern Yanzhou, then to Qiaozhou; now Qin's, Xuyi's, and Shennong commanderies were returned to Southern Yanzhou on Mingche's account.

s0211.literal: In the sixth year he entered court from Shouyang; the imperial carriage visited his mansion, bestowing bells and chimes, ten thousand hu of grain, and two thousand bolts of silk and cloth.
s0211.idiomatic: In year 6 he came to court from Shouyang; the emperor visited his house and gave bells and chimes, ten thousand hu of grain, and two thousand bolts of silk and cloth.

s0212.literal: In the seventh year he advanced to attack Pengcheng.
s0212.idiomatic: In year 7 he advanced against Pengcheng.

s0213.literal: The army reached Lüliang; Qi sent reinforcing armies numbering tens of thousands in succession; Mingche again inflicted a great defeat.
s0213.idiomatic: At Lüliang Qi sent successive reinforcements numbering tens of thousands; Mingche again routed them.

s0214.literal: In the eighth year he was advanced to Minister of Works; the rest as before.
s0214.idiomatic: In year 8 he was promoted to minister of works; the rest unchanged.

s0215.literal: Another edict said: "In former times armies set banners and clashed to the drum; recently customs have strayed, often departing from old regulations, so that in marching formations ranks are not distinguished.
s0215.idiomatic: Another edict said: "Formerly armies raised banners and fought to the drum; lately practice has strayed from the old rules, and marching formations no longer distinguish rank.

s0216.literal: Now the Minister of Works and Grand Director-General may be given battle-axes and dragon banners; subordinate generals are to receive them in descending grades."
s0216.idiomatic: Now the minister of works and grand director-general shall receive battle-axes and dragon banners; subordinate generals shall receive them by grade."

s0217.literal: Soon he was appointed director-general over military affairs in North and South Yan, North and South Qing, five provinces, and Inspector of Southern Yan Province.
s0217.idiomatic: Soon he was made director-general over North and South Yan, North and South Qing, and five provinces, and inspector of Southern Yanzhou.

s0218.literal: When Zhou extinguished Qi, Emperor Gaozong intended operations in Xu and Yan; in the ninth year an edict ordered Mingche to advance north on campaign, his heir Huizi, General of Martial Prestige in the Army and extraordinary scattered-cavalry attendant, to hold provincial affairs.
s0218.idiomatic: When Zhou destroyed Qi, Emperor Gaozong planned action in Xu and Yan; in year 9 Mingche was ordered north, his heir Huijue, army martial-prestige general and extraordinary scattered-cavalry attendant, to administer the province.

s0219.literal: Mingche's army reached Lüliang; Zhou Xuzhou overseer Liang Shiyan led Chen troops to resist; Mingche repeatedly defeated him; Shiyan withdrew to hold the city and dared not emerge.
s0219.idiomatic: At Lüliang Zhou's Xuzhou overseer Liang Shiyan led troops against him; Mingche beat him repeatedly until Shiyan shut himself in the city and would not come out.

s0220.literal: Mingche still dammed Clear Water to flood the city, ringed warcraft below the walls, and pressed the attack fiercely.
s0220.idiomatic: Mingche dammed the Clear Water to flood the city, lined ships under the walls, and pressed the assault hard.

s0221.literal: Zhou sent Grand General Wang Gui with troops to rescue.
s0221.idiomatic: Zhou sent Grand General Wang Gui to relieve the city.

s0222.literal: Gui traveled light from Clear Water into the Huai mouth, set timbers cross-current, and chained them with iron through wagon wheels, blocking the shipping route.
s0222.idiomatic: Gui came lightly from the Clear Water into the Huai mouth, laid timbers across the current, and ran iron chains through wagon wheels to block the channel.

s0223.literal: The generals heard this and were greatly alarmed; they discussed breaching the dam and withdrawing the army, loading horses onto boats.
s0223.idiomatic: The generals were alarmed and debated breaching the dam and withdrawing by boat, taking the horses aboard.

s0224.literal: Horse commander Pei Zilie argued [16]: "If we breach the dam and launch boats, the boats will surely capsize—how can that succeed?
s0224.idiomatic: Horse commander Pei Zilie argued [16]: "If we breach the dam and launch the boats, they will capsize—how can that work?

s0225.literal: Better to send the horses out ahead—that is the fitting course."
s0225.idiomatic: Better to send the horses out first—that is the safer course."

s0226.literal: Just then Mingche suffered a severe back ailment; knowing affairs would not succeed, he followed this plan and sent Xiao Mohe leading several thousand horse troops ahead.
s0226.idiomatic: Just then Mingche was gravely ill with a back complaint; seeing defeat was inevitable, he agreed and sent Xiao Mohe ahead with several thousand cavalry.

s0227.literal: Mingche still breached the dam himself, using the water's force to withdraw the army, hoping to cross.
s0227.idiomatic: Mingche still breached the dam himself, intending to ride the current downstream and escape.

s0228.literal: When they reached Qingkou the water's force gradually weakened; the ships all could not cross; the Chen army was routed; Mingche, cornered, was captured.
s0228.idiomatic: At Qingkou the current slackened; the fleet could not pass; the Chen army broke; Mingche, trapped, was taken.

s0229.literal: Soon grief and resentment brought illness; he died in Chang'an, aged sixty-seven.
s0229.idiomatic: Soon grief and resentment brought illness; he died in Chang'an at sixty-seven.

s0230.literal: In the first year of Zhide an edict said: "Li Ling's arrows were exhausted and he could not avoid requesting surrender; Yu Jin, when the waters rose, was still taken alive—thus one knows that in employing troops the superior arts are rarely met in an age.
s0230.idiomatic: In Zhide year 1 an edict said: "When Li Ling's arrows were spent he had to surrender; when the flood rose around Yu Jin he was still captured alive—truly the supreme art of war is seldom seen in any age.

s0231.literal: Former attendant-in-ordinary and minister of works, Duke of Nanping Commandery Gong Mingche, from first treading on foot,
s0231.idiomatic: The late attendant-in-ordinary and minister of works, Duke of Nanping Wu Mingche, from his first steps in service,

s0233.literal: [Till] reaching the supreme commander, [17] the marvel of a hundred battles and a hundred victories, courage to decide the moment and face death—this too matches the ancients.
s0233.idiomatic: [till] he reached supreme command, [17] with the marvel of a hundred victories and courage to decide and die—he matched the ancients.

s0234.literal: When he extended pacification over the Huai and Fei and drove far toward Peng and Bian, he overturned fierce foes like lifting hair and swept sharp armies like pouring snow; his might awed foreign customs and his achievements were recorded in our script.
s0234.idiomatic: Pacifying the Huai and Fei and driving deep toward Peng and Bian, he overturned fierce foes like plucking hair and swept elite armies like melting snow; his might awed foreign lands and his deeds were written in our script.

s0235.literal: Just when he was about to rest his chariot at Yinshan and unstrap his saddle at Huanhai, the armies went forth already aged and fate's count also ended its marvel; he did not achieve the merit of knotting the tassel and could not avoid the humiliation of entering the ward; he hoped making Feng and Xiao easy and expected pacifying Di not to be hard—though his will bent and stretched, suddenly he met frost and dew mid-course; buried grievance in a distant realm—very lamentable.
s0235.idiomatic: Just as he was to rest his chariot at Yinshan and unstrap at Huanhai, his armies grew old on campaign and fortune's tally ran out; he won no knotting-the-cord merit and could not escape the shame of captivity; he thought taking Feng and Xiao would be easy and pacifying Di not hard—yet though his will bent and straightened, frost and dew struck him suddenly; he died with grievance in a distant land—deeply to be mourned.

s0236.literal: This affair is already past and amnesties have repeatedly been proclaimed; all crimes and guilt have received sprinkling and washing, yet this lonely soul alone has not touched broad grace, so that fief and lands are submerged and sacrifices have no master.
s0236.idiomatic: That affair is past and repeated amnesties have washed all guilt, yet this lone soul alone received no grace, so his fief lies vacant and his sacrifices have no master.

s0237.literal: Recording the flawed for employment is fitting at this season; he may be posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Shaoling county state, fief one thousand households, with his son Huijue as heir."
s0237.idiomatic: To raise the flawed for service is fitting now; he is posthumously enfeoffed as marquis of Shaoling county, fief one thousand households, with his son Huijue as heir."

s0238.literal: Huijue served as gentleman of the yellow gate; for merit in pacifying Zhang Dabao he was appointed Inspector of Feng Province.
s0238.idiomatic: Huijue rose to gentleman of the yellow gate; for pacifying Zhang Dabao he was made inspector of Fengzhou.

s0240.literal: In youth he was bold and unrestrained, known for capability.
s0240.idiomatic: In youth he was bold and capable.

s0241.literal: Following Mingche on campaigns he had military merit, reaching Loyal-and-Steadfast General, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, Inspector of Gui Province, and Marquis of Runan county, fief one thousand households.
s0241.idiomatic: He campaigned with Mingche with merit, reaching loyal-and-steadfast general, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, inspector of Guizhou, and marquis of Runan with one thousand households.

s0242.literal: He died; posthumously made Inspector of Guang Province, posthumous title Jie.
s0242.idiomatic: He died; posthumously made inspector of Guangzhou, posthumous title Jie.

s0243.literal: Pei Zilie, styled Dashi, was a native of Wenxi in Hedong, son of Liang extraordinary scattered-cavalry attendant Yi.
s0243.idiomatic: Pei Zilie, styled Dashi, was from Wenxi in Hedong, son of Liang extraordinary scattered-cavalry attendant Yi.

s0244.literal: Zilie was orphaned young and had resolve.
s0244.idiomatic: Zilie lost his father young and had strong resolve.

s0245.literal: Meeting the disorders at the end of Liang, he took up martial arts and was known for fierce courage.
s0245.idiomatic: In the disorders at the end of Liang he took up arms and was known for fierce courage.

s0246.literal: He repeatedly followed Mingche on punitive campaigns, always first to scale walls and break formations.
s0246.idiomatic: He followed Mingche on campaign again and again, always first over the wall and into the line.

s0247.literal: He reached Lightning Prestige General, Administrator of North Qiao, and Interior Minister of Yueyang, Baron of Hai'an county, fief three hundred households.
s0247.idiomatic: He reached lightning-prestige general, administrator of North Qiao, interior minister of Yueyang, and baron of Hai'an with three hundred households.

s0248.literal: [18] In the fourth year of Zhide he died.

s0249.literal: The historian says: The High Ancestor ordered chaos and founded the foundation, broadly opening Heaven's fortune; Hou Tian and Ouyang Wei fully gave themselves to the Way, posts honored to the tripartite minister—beautiful.
s0249.idiomatic: The historian says: The High Ancestor quelled chaos and opened the mandate; Hou Tian and Ouyang Wei gave themselves wholly to the throne and rose to the highest offices—admirable.

s0250.literal: Wu Mingche held a commander's charge; at first he had military merit; at the Lüliang defeat it was miscalculation.
s0250.idiomatic: Wu Mingche held command; at first he won battles; at Lüliang he miscalculated.

s0251.literal: Thus his courage was not like Han Xin or Bai Qi, his wisdom unlike Sun or Wu—therefore borders were cramped, armies lost, Jinling weakened, and Zhenming fell—largely from this gradual slope.
s0251.idiomatic: His courage was not Han Xin's or Bai Qi's, his wisdom not Sun Wu's—borders shrank, armies were lost, Jinling grew weak, and Zhenming fell, largely from this beginning.

s0255.literal: [yi] the army—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, Hall editions and Comprehensive Mirror 761.
s0255.idiomatic: [yi] the army—emended per the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, and Hall editions and Comprehensive Mirror 761.

s0256.literal: Comment: the Southern History reads "to answer the righteous army."
s0256.idiomatic: Note: the Southern History reads "to answer the righteous army."

s0257.literal: Removed as bearer of the staff, Pacifies-North General—comment: in the Basic Annals of Emperor Yuan of Liang, third year of Chengsheng, first month, jiawu day, Southern Yuzhou Inspector Hou Tian was advanced to Campaign-North General; here it reads Pacifies-North General—probably an error.
s0257.idiomatic: On "removed as bearer of the staff, pacifies-north general": Liang Emperor Yuan's annals for Chengsheng year 3, first month, jiawu, advance Southern Yuzhou inspector Hou Tian to campaign-north general; pacifies-north here is probably wrong.

s0258.literal: This reads Pacifies-North General—probably an error.
s0258.idiomatic: Pacifies-north general is probably an error.

s0259.literal: Ao and his subordinate Hou Fang'er were not in accord—"Hou" in the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, Hall editions and Southern History and Comprehensive Mirror 209 and 450 all read "Marquis."
s0259.idiomatic: On "Ao and his subordinate Hou Fang'er were not in accord": the Northern Supervisory, Jigu, Hall editions, Southern History, and Comprehensive Mirror 209 and 450 read Marquis for Hou.

s0260.literal: Tian led the army to advance to Beast-barrier Isle—comment: "Beast-barrier Isle" is "Tiger-barrier Isle," changed to avoid Tang taboo.
s0260.idiomatic: On "Tian led the army to Beast-barrier Isle": Beast-barrier is Tiger-barrier, changed for Tang taboo.

s0261.literal: divided hammer-strike and halted at the tail of Wuhu Isle to await them—the Southern History lacks the three characters "divided hammer-strike."
s0261.idiomatic: On "divided hammer-strike and halted at the tail of Wuhu Isle": the Southern History lacks divided hammer-strike.

s0262.literal: Comment: the three characters "divided hammer-strike" are suspected as interpolation.
s0262.idiomatic: Note: divided hammer-strike looks like an interpolation.

s0263.literal: Or the two characters "hammer-strike" are suspected as interpolation; the old collation appended at the end of this scroll says the text may originally have read "divided halt," showing that the edition seen by Zeng Gong and others had "divided halt at the tail of Wuhu Isle."
s0263.idiomatic: Or hammer-strike is interpolated; old collation at the scroll's end says the text may read divided halt, as in editions Zeng Gong saw.

s0266.literal: "divided hammer-strike and halted at the tail of Wuhu Isle"—the text may originally have read "divided halt"—doubtful.
s0266.idiomatic: "divided hammer-strike and halted at the tail of Wuhu Isle"—or divided halt—doubtful.

s0267.literal: then entered Qi with his wife, concubines, and more than ten attendants—"then" in all editions is corrupted to "and."
s0267.idiomatic: On "then entered Qi with wife, concubines, and attendants": all editions corrupt then to and.

s0268.literal: The Hall edition's textual verification says: "Above it says Wang Lin fled to Pencheng and Chen troops would not attach to him, therefore he entered Qi—this character 'and' is a corruption for 'then.'"
s0268.idiomatic: The Hall edition notes: above, Wang Lin reached Pencheng and Chen troops would not follow, so he entered Qi—and is a corruption of then.

s0269.literal: Comment: the Southern History correctly reads "then"; now changed accordingly.
s0269.idiomatic: Note: the Southern History reads then; emended accordingly.

s0270.literal: Lan Qin's younger brother, former Inspector of High Province Yu, attacked Shixing Interior Minister Xiao Shaoji—comment: "Xiao Shaoji" in the Southern History reads "Xiao Zhaoji."
s0270.idiomatic: On "Lan Qin's brother, former High Province inspector Yu, attacked Shixing interior minister Xiao Shaoji": the Southern History reads Xiao Zhaoji.

s0271.literal: fearing the Inspector of Guangzhou would not send him—"send" was originally missing and is supplied according to all editions.
s0271.idiomatic: On "fearing the Guangzhou inspector would not send him": send was missing and is supplied from all editions.

s0272.literal: ordered one hundred taels returned to Hepu Administrator Gong Ai—comment: "Gong Ai" in the Southern History reads "Xi Ai."
s0272.idiomatic: On "ordered one hundred taels returned to Hepu administrator Gong Ai": the Southern History reads Xi Ai.

s0273.literal: Wu Mingche, styled Tongzhao—"Tongzhao" in the Southern History reads "Tongzhao" with the fire radical.
s0273.idiomatic: On "Wu Mingche, styled Tongzhao": the Southern History reads Tongzhao with the fire radical.

s0274.literal: Comment: the old collation appended at the end of this scroll says the text may originally have read "Tongzhao" with the fire radical, showing that the edition seen by Zeng Gong and others also had zhao with that radical.
s0274.idiomatic: Old collation at the scroll's end says the text may read Tongzhao with the fire radical, as in Zeng Gong's edition.

s0275.literal: Also: "Wu Mingche, styled Tongzhao"—the text may originally have read "Tongzhao" with the fire radical—doubtful.
s0275.idiomatic: Also: "Wu Mingche, styled Tongzhao"—or Tongzhao with the fire radical—doubtful.

s0276.literal: sent Prince of Ancheng Xu to console and instruct Mingche—"Xu" was originally written "taboo name"; because Yao Cha once served Chen, Chen taboo was avoided; now changed according to the Hall edition.
s0276.idiomatic: On "sent Prince of Ancheng Xu to console Mingche": Xu was written taboo name because Yao Cha served Chen; emended per the Hall edition.

s0277.literal: Mingche ordered the army further to repair siege engines—"repair" was originally missing and is supplied according to all editions.
s0277.idiomatic: On "Mingche ordered the army to repair siege engines": repair was missing and is supplied from all editions.

s0278.literal: captured Wang Lin alive and sent to the capital—"Kezhuoluo Xiaoyu" in Comprehensive Mirror, Chen Emperor Xuan's fifth year of Taijian, reads "Kezhuoluo Daoyu."
s0278.idiomatic: On "captured Wang Lin alive and sent to the capital": Comprehensive Mirror, Chen Emperor Xuan Taijian year 5, reads Kezhuoluo Daoyu for Kezhuoluo Xiaoyu.

s0279.literal: Comment: the names of Qi commanders taken prisoner in Northern Qi History and Southern History are mostly abbreviated.
s0279.idiomatic: Note: captured Qi commanders' names are mostly abbreviated in the Northern Qi History and Southern History.

s0280.literal: Comprehensive Mirror 368 also reads "Xiaoyu"; Comprehensive Mirror reads "Daoyu"—the basis is unknown.
s0280.idiomatic: Comprehensive Mirror 368 also has Xiaoyu; another passage has Daoyu—the basis is unknown.

s0281.literal: bold warriors racing—"warrior" in the Northern Supervisory and Hall editions reads "tiger."
s0281.idiomatic: On "bold warriors racing": the Northern Supervisory and Hall editions read tiger for warrior.

s0282.literal: Comment: this was changed to avoid Tang taboo.

s0283.literal: An edict sent Palace Usher Xiao Chunfeng—"Xiao Chunfeng" in the Southern History reads "Xiao Chun."
s0283.idiomatic: On "edict sent palace usher Xiao Chunfeng": the Southern History reads Xiao Chun.

s0284.literal: Horse commander Pei Zilie argued—"horse commander" in the Southern History reads "horse bright garrison."
s0284.idiomatic: On "horse commander Pei Zilie argued": the Southern History reads horse bright garrison.

s0285.literal: Comment: Comprehensive Mirror, Chen Emperor Xuan's tenth year of Taijian, reads "horse commander"; Examination of Variants says the Southern History reads "horse bright commander"—now following the Book of Chen.
s0285.idiomatic: Comprehensive Mirror, Chen Emperor Xuan Taijian year 10, reads horse commander; Examination of Variants says the Southern History reads horse bright commander—following the Book of Chen.

s0287.literal: [Till] reaching the supreme commander—changed according to the Northern Supervisory and Hall editions.
s0287.idiomatic: [Till] reaching the supreme commander—emended per the Northern Supervisory and Hall editions.

s0288.literal: fief three hundred households—all editions read "five hundred households."
s0288.idiomatic: On "fief three hundred households": all editions read five hundred households.
